questions.stem: The main feature that distinguishes monopolistic competition from perfect competition is

options.text: the number of firms in the industry
the existence of barriers to entry

questions.explanation: Both structures have many firms and free entry, and both leave firms with only normal profit in the long run. The one thing that changes is that products are differentiated by brand, packaging, quality or location, which is what gives each firm slight control over its own price.

distractorRationale.a: Both structures are characterised by a large number of firms
distractorRationale.c: Entry is free in both; barriers belong to oligopoly and monopoly
distractorRationale.d: Free entry means only normal profit survives in the long run under both structures

questions.stem: Heavy advertising is a normal feature of monopolistic competition because

options.text: firms must persuade buyers that their brand differs from close substitutes
there are only a few firms in the industry
buyers have perfect knowledge of all prices
the government requires firms to publicise their prices

questions.explanation: Differentiation only earns a firm loyal customers if buyers believe in it. Advertising builds that belief, which shifts the firm's demand curve outwards and makes it less elastic. Under perfect competition, where goods are identical, advertising would be pure waste.

distractorRationale.b: A few firms describes oligopoly; monopolistic competition has many firms
distractorRationale.c: Perfect knowledge is an assumption of perfect competition, where advertising is pointless
distractorRationale.d: There is no such requirement; advertising here is a commercial strategy, not a legal duty

questions.stem: A market dominated by only two large firms is called
questions.explanation: Duopoly is the special case of oligopoly with exactly two sellers. Interdependence is at its sharpest here, since each firm need only watch one rival to predict the whole market's reaction.

distractorRationale.b: A bilateral monopoly is one seller facing one buyer, which is a different situation
distractorRationale.c: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, not two sellers
distractorRationale.d: A cartel is a formal agreement among firms to fix price or output, which may or may not involve only two firms

questions.stem: Prices in an oligopolistic market tend to remain unchanged for long periods mainly because

options.text: each firm fears that a price cut will be matched by rivals while a price rise will not be followed
the government fixes the price of the product by law
the firms face perfectly elastic demand curves
production costs in oligopolistic industries never change

questions.explanation: This is the reasoning behind the kinked demand curve. A price cut is matched, so the firm gains few extra customers but earns less on each sale. A price rise is not matched, so the firm loses customers to rivals. Both directions look unattractive, so the price stays put and competition shifts to advertising instead.

distractorRationale.b: Price rigidity in oligopoly arises from the firms' own strategic caution, not from legislation
distractorRationale.c: Perfectly elastic demand belongs to the price taker in perfect competition
distractorRationale.d: Costs certainly do change; rigidity means prices fail to follow those cost changes promptly

questions.stem: An agreement among a few large firms to fix output and price so as to act like a single seller is known as
questions.explanation: A cartel is collusion between independent firms which continue to exist separately but coordinate price or output quotas to raise joint profit. OPEC, of which Nigeria has been a member since 1971, allocates production quotas to its members in exactly this way.

distractorRationale.b: A merger fuses firms into one legal entity, so they no longer need to agree with each other
distractorRationale.c: A subsidy is a government payment to producers and has nothing to do with collusion
distractorRationale.d: A conglomerate is a single firm operating in unrelated industries

questions.stem: In which market structure does the individual firm have absolutely no control over the price of its product?
questions.explanation: Only the perfectly competitive firm is a pure price taker. Its output is a negligible share of total supply and its product is identical to everyone else's, so it must accept the ruling price. In each of the other three structures the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve and therefore has some price-setting power.

distractorRationale.a: Brand loyalty gives a monopolistically competitive firm slight control over price
distractorRationale.b: An oligopolist has considerable power over price, though it is constrained by rivals' reactions
distractorRationale.d: The monopolist has the greatest control of all, limited only by market demand

questions.stem: In the long run, a firm under monopolistic competition earns only normal profit.
questions.explanation: True. Entry into monopolistic competition is free, so abnormal profit attracts new brands. Each newcomer takes a slice of the existing firms' custom until profit falls to the normal level. Differentiation gives a firm control over price, but it does not protect its profit.

distractorRationale.b: This confuses monopolistic competition with monopoly, where blocked entry allows abnormal profit to persist

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following are forms of non-price competition typically used by oligopolists?

options.text: Extended warranties and free after-sales service
Selling below average variable cost indefinitely
Attractive packaging and frequent product restyling
Publishing a schedule of discounted prices every week

questions.explanation: Non-price competition means attracting customers by any means other than cutting price. Advertising, warranties and after-sales service, and packaging or restyling all fit, because each raises the perceived value of the product while leaving the price alone.

distractorRationale.c: Selling below average variable cost indefinitely would bankrupt the firm and is not a competitive strategy
distractorRationale.e: Publishing weekly discounts is price competition, the very thing oligopolists try to avoid
